title: Why compound interest wins
blurb: Interest lands on top of interest, so money grows faster the longer it sits. You'll see what $1,000 does at 8% a year, and the one-line trick for knowing when it doubles.
takeaway: You learned why time matters more than amount.

cards.body: Compound interest means you earn interest on your interest. Money grows faster the longer it sits.
Put $1,000 in an account paying 8% a year. Twelve months later it has grown by $80.
$1,000 at 8% a year. Year 1 you earn $80. Year 2 you earn $86 — because now the $80 is earning too.
The rule of 72: divide 72 by the rate to see how many years it takes to double. At 8%, that's 9 years.
Two students both put away $200 a month. One starts at 18, the other at 28. By 60 the early one ends up with roughly twice as much.
Same $200 a month either way. The early start just hands interest more years to pile on itself.
Starting at 18 instead of 28 can roughly double what you end up with. Time matters more than amount.

cards.question: Why does year 2 earn more than year 1?
choices: The rate goes up each year
cards.why: Interest is added to your balance, so the next year is worked out on a bigger number.

title: Your first budget in 4 lines
blurb: A budget is a plan you make before you spend, not a punishment you write after. Four lines is enough to start, and one of them does most of the work.
takeaway: You learned that the savings line should move on its own.

cards.body: A budget is just a plan for money before you spend it. Four lines is enough to start.
Half goes to needs — rent, food, the bus. That's the 50.
Thirty percent is wants. Not a moral failing, just a planned amount.
The last fifth is savings. That's the line that actually changes anything.
Track one month before you set the numbers. Most people are shocked by one category, and that category is your lever.
Automate the savings line. If it moves on payday, you never have to be disciplined.

cards.question: Why automate savings instead of saving what's left over?
choices: Banks pay more on automatic transfers
Nothing is left over at the end of the month
cards.why: Money you can see is money you spend. Moving it first makes the plan happen without willpower.

title: What an emergency fund is for
blurb: The point of an emergency fund is not the interest. It's that a flat tyre stops being a crisis and starts being an errand.
takeaway: You learned what cash is for when something breaks.

cards.body: An emergency fund is cash you keep boring on purpose. Not invested, not locked up. Just there.
A $400 repair with the cash there is an errand. You pay it and forget it.
The same $400 on a card at 24% is a crisis that follows you into June.
Start with $500. That covers most of what actually goes wrong: a phone, a tyre, a co-pay.
An emergency fund buys you the right to say no to bad borrowing.

cards.question: Why keep an emergency fund in plain cash instead of investing it?
choices: You need it on the day you need it
Investing it is against the rules
cards.why: Investments can be down exactly when your car breaks. The job of this money is to be available, not to grow.

title: Credit scores, plainly
blurb: A credit score is a guess about whether you pay people back. Two of the five inputs do most of the work, and both are in your control.
takeaway: You learned that paying on time beats paying it all.

cards.body: A credit score is one number that guesses how likely you are to pay back what you borrow.
It runs from about 300 to 850. Most people sit somewhere in the middle.
Paying on time is the heaviest input by a distance. One late mark costs you for years.
Second is how much of your limit you use. Under 30% is the usual advice; under 10% is better.
Paying on time is worth more than paying it all off. One late payment costs more than a big balance.

cards.question: You can only do one this month. Which helps your score more?
choices: Pay the full balance a week late
cards.why: Payment history is the heaviest single input. A late mark sits on your report for years; a carried balance does not.

title: Good debt, bad debt
blurb: Debt isn't good or bad by nature. It's a price you pay for time, and the question is only ever whether you're buying something worth more than the price.
takeaway: You learned to ask what the debt buys before you take it.

cards.body: All debt is renting money. The interest rate is the rent.
Rent is worth paying when the thing you bought is worth more later — a degree, a business.
It almost never is when the thing shrinks: a night out, a phone, a weekend.
Ask one question: will this still be worth something when I finish paying for it?

cards.question: A credit card charges 24% a year. A savings account pays 4%. What should a spare $100 do first?
cards.why: Paying off 24% debt is a guaranteed 24% return. No savings account can beat that.

title: Why index funds beat picking
blurb: Most professional stock pickers lose to a fund that buys everything and thinks about nothing. Here's why that keeps happening.
takeaway: You learned why the boring fund keeps winning.

cards.body: An index fund buys a slice of every company on a list, then does nothing else.
Picking one company means being right about that one, twice, for twenty years.
Over twenty years most professional pickers land behind the boring fund. Fees eat the difference.
The boring fund wins because it costs almost nothing and never panics.

cards.question: Why do fees matter so much over 20 years?
choices: Fees come out of the money that would have compounded
cards.why: Every dollar in fees is a dollar that stops earning. Over decades a 1% fee quietly takes a large slice of the total.

title: Stoicism: control what you can
blurb: The Stoics split the world in two and told you to spend your energy on one half. It's two thousand years old and it maps almost exactly onto a bad exam week.
takeaway: You learned to spend your energy on the half you control.

cards.body: Stoics split the world in two: things you control, and things you don't.
Your effort and your reaction are the first group. Those are always yours.
A posted grade, a curve, what somebody else scored — second group. Epictetus said suffering comes from trying to control those.
A grade is already up. Refreshing the page is the second group. Emailing to ask what you missed is the first.
Before you stress, ask: is this in my control? If no, let it go. If yes, act on it today.

cards.question: Which of these is in the first group — the part you control?
cards.why: Your effort is yours. The curve and other people's scores are outcomes you can influence at best, never control.

title: The Socratic method
blurb: Socrates never told anyone the answer. He asked until they noticed they didn't have one — which turns out to be the fastest way to find out what you actually know.
takeaway: You learned that asking why beats reading again.

cards.body: Socrates taught by asking questions, not giving answers. Start with something you believe.
Ask why once and you get a reason. That part is usually easy.
Ask why twice and most beliefs run out of floor. That is not a failure — that's the method working.
Asking why this is the answer beats rereading the answer.

cards.question: Why does asking 'why' beat rereading your notes?
choices: It forces you to produce the reason instead of recognise it
cards.why: Recognising something feels like knowing it. Producing the reason from memory is the thing a test actually asks for.

title: Occam's razor
blurb: The oldest debugging tool there is: when two explanations both fit, start with the one that assumes less. It isn't a law of nature, and that matters too.
takeaway: You learned which explanation to test first.

cards.body: Occam's razor: when two explanations fit the same facts, start with the one that assumes less.
Your code broke after you changed one line. That line is one assumption.
A compiler bug is four. It might still be right — it is just more expensive to check.
The simplest explanation isn't the truest. It's the one worth checking first.

cards.question: What does the razor actually tell you to do?
cards.why: It ranks what to check, not what is true. A complicated explanation can still win once the simple one fails.

title: The veil of ignorance
blurb: John Rawls' test for whether a rule is fair: design it before you know who you'll be under it.
takeaway: You learned a test for whether a rule is actually fair.

cards.body: John Rawls asked: what rules would you write if you didn't know who you'd be under them?
You keep everything you know about how the world works. You lose only who you are in it.
Then you get handed a life at random and have to live under the rule you just wrote.
Would you set the late-work policy the same way if you didn't know whether you'd be the student with a job after school?
A fair rule is one you'd still write if you didn't know which side of it you'd land on.

cards.question: What is the veil hiding from you?
choices: Which position in society you'll occupy
cards.why: You keep full knowledge of how the world works. You lose only the knowledge of who you'll be in it.

title: The map is not the territory
blurb: Every model leaves things out on purpose. Trouble starts when you forget which things.
takeaway: You learned to ask what a model left out.

cards.body: A map is useful because it leaves things out. A map with everything on it would be the size of the world.
Every model does this: a formula, a stereotype, a study guide. Something got cut to make it usable.
The skill is knowing what was cut — and whether you needed it.
A practice test predicts your real score well. It still can't tell you that you always slow down on the last section.
Ask what a model left out before you trust what it says.

cards.question: What makes a map useful?
choices: It leaves the right things out
cards.why: Detail is what makes a map unusable. The skill is knowing which detail was dropped and whether you needed it.

title: Spaced practice beats cramming
blurb: Same total hours, very different results. Splitting study across days works because forgetting a little is part of how remembering gets strong.
takeaway: You learned that the gap between sessions does the work.

cards.body: One long cram goes in fast and leaks just as fast. A week later almost none of it is there.
Split the same hour over six days and every session catches the memory just before it goes.
Your brain strengthens a memory each time it nearly forgets it, then pulls it back.
The gap between sessions is doing the work, not the sessions.

cards.question: Why does leaving a gap between study sessions help?
choices: Partly forgetting makes the recall count for more
cards.why: Effortful recall is what strengthens a memory. If nothing was forgotten, there is nothing to recall.

title: How to study for a science quiz
blurb: Science quizzes ask you to explain a mechanism, not to recognise a term. Three passes over two evenings does more than one long night with a highlighter.
takeaway: You learned to draw the mechanism instead of highlighting it.

cards.body: A science quiz almost never asks you to recognise a word. Highlighting the definition feels like work and isn't.
Draw the mechanism instead: two sides, which one is saltier, and which way the water goes.
If you can draw it from memory, you can answer any wording of the question.
Don't memorise 'osmosis: movement of water'. Draw the two sides, mark which is saltier, then draw the arrow.
If you can draw the mechanism from memory, you're ready. Highlighting is not studying.

cards.question: You have two evenings before the quiz. What's the better use of night one?
choices: Write what you remember, then check
cards.why: Writing it first shows you the gaps. Rereading shows you familiar pages and hides what you don't know.

title: Active recall in ten minutes
blurb: The single highest-value ten minutes in studying, and it needs no app, no cards, and no colour coding.
takeaway: You learned to start with a blank page, every time.

cards.body: Active recall means pulling something out of your head, not putting it back in.
The whole method: close everything, write what you remember, then check what you missed.
The part you missed is your entire study list. Everything else is already learned.
Blank page first, notes second. Always in that order.

cards.question: Rereading your notes feels much easier than a blank page. Why is that a warning sign?
choices: Easy means you already know it
Recognising is easier than remembering, and only one is tested
Notes are shorter than the textbook
cards.why: Familiarity feels like knowledge. A blank page is uncomfortable precisely because it measures the thing a test measures.

title: Mix the problems up
blurb: Doing twenty of the same problem type teaches you to run one method. Mixing them teaches you to pick one — which is the harder half.
takeaway: You learned to practise choosing the method, not just running it.

cards.body: Most problem sets are blocked: four of type A, then four of type B.
That trains running a method. Mixing them up trains choosing one, which is the harder half.
On the test nothing is labelled. Practise the part that isn't labelled.
Do 5 of A, 5 of B, then shuffle 10 together. The shuffled ten are where the test actually lives.
On the test nothing is labelled. Practise the part that isn't labelled.

cards.question: Why does mixed practice feel worse than blocked practice?
choices: You make more mistakes while you're learning to choose
cards.why: Struggling to pick the right method is the skill being built. The mistakes are the training, not a sign it isn't working.

title: How to read a chapter once
blurb: Reading a chapter twice is usually reading it badly once, twice. Three moves make one pass enough.
takeaway: You learned to read once, with a question in hand.

cards.body: Before reading, turn every heading into a question. 'Cell division' becomes 'how does a cell divide?'
Now you're searching for an answer instead of scanning a page, and you notice it when it arrives.
At the end, write four sentences with the book shut. That's your whole set of notes.
Reading twice is slower than reading once and answering.

cards.question: Why turn headings into questions before you read?
choices: It gives you something to be looking for
cards.why: A question turns reading from scanning into searching. You notice the answer when it arrives, instead of noticing nothing.

title: The five-minute start
blurb: Procrastination is nearly always about starting, not about working. So make starting the only thing you commit to.
takeaway: You learned to commit to starting and let finishing follow.

cards.body: Putting something off is almost always about starting it, not about doing it.
So shrink the commitment to five minutes, and mean the part where you're allowed to stop.
Most of the time you don't stop. Starting was the hard part and it's behind you.
For an essay, the five minutes is opening the file and writing a bad first sentence. Bad is fine. It gets deleted.
Commit to starting, never to finishing. Finishing takes care of itself more often than you'd think.

cards.question: Why does the five minutes have to be a real permission to stop?
choices: Five minutes is enough for most work
If it's a trick, your brain stops falling for it
cards.why: The method works because starting is genuinely cheap. If stopping isn't allowed, starting costs the whole task again.
